extracted.intended_audience: litigators, judges, legal counsel for news agencies and media companies
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evidentiary/procedural principles for litigation about news-wire 'tips' (taking/copying news from rival wire services), confidentiality of wire-service contracts, and equitable relief. Focuses on what practices are wrongful, what proof is required, and how courts treat customary practice and affidavits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to take tips from each other's wires
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether either news service had a legal right to take 'tips' from the other's wire; defendant's counsel denies that either had any such right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court framed the central legal proposition as whether either party had a right to take tips from the other's wire — this is the core issue the hearing focuses on. Counsel dispute whether any permissive right exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of material from early editions and bulletin boards
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether material taken from early newspaper editions or bulletin boards may be used by another service (copying the words vs reporting it as a rumor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court observed that taking something off a bulletin board does not necessarily undermine a theory of wrongdoing and questioned practical differences between copying text ('The Pope died at eight p.m.') and reporting a rumor ('It is rumored the Pope died'). Timeliness constraints (early-morning editions) may make verification impracticable and thus affect whether re-use is treated as independent reporting or appropriation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surreptitious taking of tips is wrongful
rubrics_metrics.description: Surreptitious appropriation of tips off a rival's wire is improper — counsel characterized taking tips off the other's wire as 'surreptitious.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court indicated no one contends a party has a right to take tips surreptitiously off another's wires; such conduct may bar equitable relief for the taker and is treated as morally and legally suspect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Custom and long-standing practice may bar equitable relief
rubrics_metrics.description: A widespread custom or habitual practice of taking tips between services may be a defense and could bar the complainant from equitable relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counsel argued practice was common and overwhelming (affidavits of managers). The Court noted that habitual practice might bar relief in equity, so proof of custom is a potentially dispositive fact to be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stealing a tip is morally equivalent to stealing the whole story
rubrics_metrics.description: "The stealing of the tip is just as iniquitous as the stealing of the whole story," though the extent of injury may differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle was urged by counsel to emphasize culpability even when only a 'tip' (brief lead or essential fact) is taken; court must weigh injury magnitude separately from wrongdoing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of systematic appropriation requires corroborated affidavits and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegations that a defendant systematically took tips must be supported by affidavits and concrete instances (e.g., Cleveland example, bonuses for stealing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complainant relied on numerous affidavits and a 'pretty overwhelming case' showing a system (examples of operators stealing from wires, payment of bonuses). The Court allowed rebuttal affidavits but warned against excessive voluminous filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidential contractual relations for wire services
rubrics_metrics.description: Contracts may provide that news sent to a paper or service be used confidentially and only for the recipient's service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counsel proposed to file an affidavit showing the Cleveland contract required confidential use; such contractual confidentiality is relevant to claims and remedies (supports inequity of appropriation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable protection of contractual relations may differ from other counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether contractual relations (confidential use agreements) can be protected in a court of equity is a distinct and important question, separate from other claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court noted this is 'quite different' from other counts and may be determinative; parties were invited to brief the authorities on whether equity can enforce such confidential contractual relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest from employing the same individual for competing services
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the same person (e.g., telegraph editor/operator) to serve competing wire services creates temptation and conflict, and is business-policy questionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court and counsel observed that having the same man 'serving three masters' or employed by both services invites leak/appropriation and is relevant both to liability and to credibility of explanations about how news was gathered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between wholesale copying and rewriting after verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a service 'took the stories bodily' or merely used them as the basis for independent verification and rewrite affects culpability, but practical timing may erase the distinction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complainant argued defendants 'took the stories and sent the stories themselves'; defendants claimed they investigated and rewrote. The Court noted that early-edition timing often makes full independent verification impracticable, making the legal distinction less credible in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural limits on affidavits and scope of rebuttal
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits should be confined to rebuttal matter; the court may limit further affidavits if filings become voluminous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court indicated it 'probably shall not allow any more affidavits' beyond rebuttal, analogizing to practice in title cases, and instructed parties to submit affidavits and briefs on set schedules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and scheduling for service of affidavits and briefs
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties must serve rebutting affidavits and file briefs according to court-directed deadlines (e.g., affidavits to be served on Monday; briefs within a week thereafter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical scheduling was set during the hearing: afford each side an opportunity to serve rebuttal affidavits and then file briefs within specified short timeframes; counsel requested reasonable notice to prepare replies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctity of news gathering and prohibition against 'pirating' news with news value
rubrics_metrics.description: A manager's asserted principle: preserve the sanctity of news gathered by associations and oppose pirating or appropriating such news so long as it has news value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Melville E. Stone's affidavit emphasizes a consistent policy against appropriation/piracy of gathered news, presenting this normative standard as a basis for the complainant's equitable claims and moral argument.
